Structured

Part 1: Algorithms
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
•
Explain what an algorithm is.
•
Identify the three fundamental control structures used in
structured programming.
•
Explain how sequence, selection, and iteration change the
flow of a program.

Before Structured Programming
Early programs often relied on the GOTO statement, which allowed the program
to jump directly to any labeled line of code.
While this made simple programs possible, larger programs often became
confusing because execution could jump unpredictably between many
different locations.
In the 1960s and 1970s, structured programming replaced this approach by
using sequence, selection (if statements), and iteration (loops), making
programs easier to read, test, and maintain.

Structured Programming
Structured programming organizes programs using predictable control
structures instead of jumping unpredictably between different sections of
code.
The three fundamental control structures are:
Sequence — Perform instructions in order.
Selection — Choose which instructions to perform.
Iteration — Repeat instructions.
These structures make programs easier to read, test, and maintain.

Algorithms
An algorithm is a sequence of step-by-step instructions designed to perform a
task or solve a problem.
Programs are implementations of algorithms using a programming language.
Algorithms often:
• Receive input.
• Process that information.
• Produce output.
• Use control structures to determine which steps happen and when.
